kp.k: AI challenges apprenticeship as the default training model
kp.d: McCormack endorses Ethan Mollick’s reported assertion that AI has broken apprenticeship-based professional training because it is already useful to both juniors and seniors. She describes law’s traditional formation process as repeated assignments and variable feedback over hundreds or thousands of hours, and calls for law schools and practicing organizations to rethink their respective responsibilities. This is an argument reported from an interview and endorsed by the hosts, not a measured finding about training outcomes.
qs: “The apprenticeship model broke this summer. It’s broken. It doesn’t work anymore.”
Because it’s already useful for juniors in any profession, but it’s also useful for senior-level lawyers or bankers or consultants

And you and I have talked before about what part of that is the responsibility of law schools, and what part of that is the responsibility of practicing lawyers in law firms or other legal organizations.

kp.k: Deliberate coaching should replace incidental learning through repetition
kp.d: Using sports and music as analogies, McCormack advocates structured, deliberately sequenced practice rather than imitation. Leonard argues that junior lawyers historically received repetitive practice in research and drafting without consistent coaching or explanations of how assignments served clients. They propose combining practice, coaching and learning science in a redesigned training model; they do not present evidence that such a legal training model has already succeeded.
qs: She wasn’t like, “Just follow me, just swim how I swim.” That wasn’t what she did. It was really like a specific training program.
What you didn’t have was the intentionality of the coaching.
we need a new approach that incorporates coaching and science and the practice.

kp.k: Custom GPTs offer experimental simulation-based arbitrator training
kp.d: McCormack describes personally building a custom GPT for one module of AAA’s Arbitration Fundamentals course, which uses a hypothetical case, live instruction and team exercises. Her prototype introduces personas that challenge new arbitrators and generates suggestions for further training tools. This is an exploratory personal experiment, with no reported deployment or learner-outcome evaluation; Leonard expresses interest in an analogous associate-training GPT.
qs: I started playing with building a custom GPT for one of the modules covered in that course.
The course is live, with a hypothetical case that the learners follow from beginning to end, stopping and starting in different modules and working in teams.
I’ve created some personas, and they’re giving the learner (a new arbitrator) some challenges.
I don’t know what will come of it exactly, but I’m excited about what we could build in terms of our education products at the AAA.

kp.k: Billing incentives shaped apprenticeship and constrain training redesign
kp.d: Leonard argues that corporate clients historically underwrote junior associate training through paid work and that firms valued associate retention partly for continued revenue generation. McCormack contrasts this with in-house teams, reporting conversations about creative training on longstanding matters and suggesting their cost-center economics make investing time in custom GPT training financially sensible. These are the hosts’ economic interpretation and practitioner observations, without quantified comparisons.
qs: Because the reason that we had an apprenticeship model is because it’s underwritten by corporate clients who had to put up with training junior-level associates.
They were paying for those hours, so it made economic sense.
I hear in-house legal teams putting together pretty creative training processes on long-standing matters.
It makes sense that they can spend the time building a custom GPT for a training set for the new lawyers that are cycling onto a matter.

kp.k: AI-enabled education can raise expectations rather than ban tools
kp.d: The hosts report Mollick’s account of redesigning Wharton teaching when moving from GPT-3.5 to 4.0, which he characterized as making AI as smart as his students. McCormack describes incorporating AI as teammate, mentor and challenger. Leonard reports that entrepreneurship students moved from producing a pitch deck and business plan over a semester to an MVP by the end of the second week; McCormack also recounts prototyping within one class and using AI users for testing. They treat this cross-domain example as inspiration for legal education, not evidence of equivalent legal outcomes.

So instead, he builds it in as a teammate, and as a mentor, and as someone who challenges the students in their work.
And now, by the end of the second week, they have to come up with an MVP for a product—because now they’re able to prototype.
He said, like, within one class they can have an MVP and then create a bunch of AI users to test it and try and break it and give it feedback.

kp.k: Uneven capabilities require experimentation and continuing engagement
kp.d: McCormack recounts Mollick’s 'jagged frontier' framework: AI capabilities are uneven and can surprise users in either direction, while human capabilities also vary. Leonard warns that lawyers can become anchored to outdated assumptions about what AI can do. She argues that opting out can mean losing opportunities to improve work and surrendering influence over the technology’s development; this is a recommendation and forecast rather than a documented competitive effect.
qs: you don’t really know what it can do and what it can’t do until you try and see if it can do it.
Humans have jagged edges of capabilities, which is so true.
I think part of the challenge of working with lawyers is they get stuck on the idea that it can only do this set of things, when it’s constantly developing new capabilities.
you’re not taking an active part in shaping it, and you’re handing over the control of the future and how it’s shaped to people that you don’t know or don’t trust.

kp.k: Source highlighting can reduce human verification effort
kp.d: Leonard reports that ChatGPT Deep Research citations now open source websites and highlight supporting passages, making her fact-checking faster than searching entire pages. She is uncertain whether the feature is genuinely new, and McCormack has not yet observed it herself. Leonard uses this experience to suggest that even anticipated verification jobs may change quickly; neither host claims that highlighting eliminates the need for human checking or supplies a measured error reduction.
qs: But now the citations are inline in the report (maybe they always were, I’m not sure), and when I click one now, it actually pulls up the website and highlights where it found the information.
That is amazing to me, because before I was clicking the URL to see if it was hallucinating and having to do a lot more fact-checking.
And maybe that’s still true, but a week ago I thought fact-checking was something different than it’s already become.

kp.k: Hosts recommend ambitious experimentation beyond document summarization
kp.d: The hosts favor testing larger applications rather than restricting adoption to small summarization pilots, drawing partly on Mollick’s reported advice. Leonard cites a Georgia firm’s reported $7.2 million verdict using ChatGPT deep research as an illustrative story, without providing case details or evidence isolating AI’s contribution. She also uses siloed city-government departments as an analogy for the potential public benefits of integrating and analyzing information across systems.

kp.k: Reported Harvey associates illustrate AI-integrated professional formation
kp.d: McCormack attributes to Meghan Ma at Stanford the view that Harvey is reshaping junior-lawyer training and development, with 'Harvey associates' incorporating the platform into their routine work. She also describes strongly positive and negative professional reactions and interprets this attention as a sign of market breakthrough. These are secondhand observations and her interpretation, not adoption statistics, evaluated training outcomes or firsthand product experience.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe AI as changing legal training, accelerating research verification, enabling integrated legal workflows, and creating both public-service opportunities and risks of unequal access.
pts.d:
1. Bridget McCormack reports experimenting with a custom GPT for an AAA arbitration-training module, including personas that challenge learners. She sees potential for AI-enhanced, hands-on education but does not report a completed or validated training product. Jen Leonard proposes extending this approach to associate development through deliberate practice and coaching.
2. McCormack explicitly endorses Ethan Mollick's reported argument that AI has broken apprenticeship-based professional training because it is useful to both junior and senior professionals. Leonard argues that the traditional legal apprenticeship model supplied repetition without consistent intentional coaching and depended economically on corporate clients paying for junior work. Their proposed response is to redesign training around practice, coaching and a more systematic understanding of learning. The original declaration that apprenticeship 'broke this summer' belongs to Mollick, as quoted in the episode, rather than originating with either speaker.
3. Leonard reports that ChatGPT Deep Research's source highlighting makes her fact-checking substantially faster. She suggests that even verification work, which she had imagined as a future human task, is already changing. This is a claim about accelerating human checking, not eliminating it.
4. Leonard predicts that Harvey's partnerships with LexisNexis and iManage could overcome barriers to legal adoption by combining AI, high-quality legal information and documents in lawyers' existing workflows. She suggests the iManage integration could help preserve data protections and client protocols. McCormack argues that integrating LexisNexis and Shepard's could reduce the need to switch platforms to check citations before submitting legal work. Both frame the combination as potentially important for next-generation practice.
5. Leonard says Harvey is focused on BigLaw, citing reports from small firms unable to obtain subscriptions. She raises the possibility that unequal access could widen a divide between well-resourced and less-resourced providers rather than democratize legal services. McCormack and Leonard speculate about future consumer or jurisdiction-specific subscriptions; neither reports such offerings as available.
6. McCormack predicts that comparable tools could help courts conduct initial reviews and improve service to the public, including in consequential family matters. Leonard argues that BigLaw pro bono practices could use integrated AI to scale assistance, and McCormack recommends engineers collaborating with clinics, legal-services offices and courts to build reusable solutions rather than handle only individual cases. These are opportunities and recommendations, not measured outcomes.
7. Leonard argues that lawyers should pursue more ambitious uses than summarization, citing a reported Georgia firm's $7.2 million verdict involving ChatGPT Deep Research. She also warns that refusing to engage with AI can mean foregoing capability gains and relinquishing influence over how the technology develops.
8. The episode relays Meghan Ma's reported observation that Harvey is reshaping junior-lawyer training and producing 'Harvey associates' whose workflows incorporate it. This is a secondhand attributed claim, not McCormack's own observation of Harvey use.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists mainly of personal experimentation, professional experience, reported conversations, partnership announcements and secondhand examples; the transcript provides no quantitative evaluation of legal training or workflow improvements.
pts.d:
1. McCormack's training claim rests on her own early custom-GPT experiment, having taken AAA's Arbitration Fundamentals course, and her experience with clinical legal education. Leonard and McCormack draw on their experience of junior-lawyer training. The sports and music examples are analogies for deliberate practice, not evidence of AI's effectiveness in legal education.
2. The apprenticeship-disruption argument relies substantially on an interview with Mollick and the speakers' endorsement and interpretation of it. McCormack also reports conversations with in-house teams developing creative training processes. No longitudinal data on lawyer competence, staffing or apprenticeship outcomes are presented.
3. The verification-speed claim rests on Leonard's direct experience using Deep Research. She is unsure whether source highlighting is newly introduced. There is no measured time saving or hallucination-rate comparison. References to Deep Research doing well on tests and hallucinating less are nonspecific; the episode names no benchmark or result supporting them.
4. The integration claims rest on the announced Harvey–LexisNexis and Harvey–iManage partnerships and the speakers' interpretation of their potential. McCormack also mentions asking ChatGPT how the integrations work. She explicitly discloses that she has never used Harvey. The transcript provides no direct test of integrated citation checking, security compliance or productivity.
5. The unequal-access concern is supported by Leonard's account of small-firm discussion on social media, not subscription or market-share data. Predictions about consumer access, courts and scalable pro bono are speculative extensions of the described capabilities.
6. The Georgia verdict is a reported case example used to illustrate ambitious AI use. The transcript supplies neither the case name nor details establishing AI's contribution to the outcome. The 'Harvey associates' observation is attributed secondhand to Meghan Ma, without underlying study details.
7. McCormack interprets strong professional reactions to Harvey as a sign of market breakthrough. This is expressly an inference from attention and sentiment rather than demonstrated product performance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current experiences and recently announced integrations are distinguished from open-ended predictions; most proposed educational and public-interest benefits depend on further design, access and implementation.
pts.d:
1. In this 2025 episode, McCormack describes the arbitration GPT as a current personal experiment begun after the previous episode. She does not know what will result from it. Redesigned associate training remains a proposal, with no implementation deadline. Mollick's quoted 'this summer' is a relative timeframe not anchored to a precise date in the supplied transcript.
2. Leonard's verification observation concerns her recent research work. McCormack guesses the feature may have rolled out in the previous week, while Leonard explicitly allows that it may have existed earlier. Faster checking does not establish that citations can be relied upon without human verification.
3. The speakers describe the Lexis partnership as announced the previous week and the two Harvey partnerships as announced within roughly six weeks. Claimed benefits are variously described as potential, apparent or inferred, rather than fully demonstrated. Leonard qualifies her understanding of the distinction between the strategic Lexis partnership and the more technical iManage connection.
4. Public-interest and consumer benefits are conditional on affordable access, suitable document infrastructure, possible subscription tiers or alternative providers. Neither speaker knows Harvey's relevant pricing or plans. The risk of a widening divide is explicitly conditional on advanced access remaining concentrated in BigLaw.
5. Court and scalable pro bono applications have no specified delivery date. They depend on institutions and engineers building and trying solutions. Leonard expects technology costs generally to fall, but offers no schedule or specific price forecast.
6. The broader recommendation to rethink training and pursue ambitious applications is immediate, reflecting the speakers' view that capabilities are already changing faster than many lawyers recognize.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes affect learners, educators, law firms and legal departments, with uneven access potentially shaping benefits for small firms, public-interest providers, courts and unrepresented people.
pts.d:
1. New arbitrators, law students and junior associates are potential recipients of AI-enabled simulations, challenges and deliberate practice. Senior lawyers, mentors, law schools, AAA and other training organizations would need to rethink how professional competence is developed rather than relying on accumulated billable repetition.
2. Law firms face questions about apprenticeship economics and how they produce experienced lawyers. Corporate clients historically financed junior training through paid hours. In-house legal departments, as buyer-side cost centers rather than law-firm revenue centers, are described as having different incentives to invest in efficient matter-specific training.
3. Practicing lawyers using research tools may spend less time locating source material and switching systems for citation checks. Firms and corporate legal departments using iManage, and existing Harvey and Lexis customers in particular, are positioned as likely beneficiaries of integration. Protection of client data and attorney work product is a central adoption concern.
4. BigLaw firms are described as the principal current Harvey market. Small firms, legal-services organizations and consumers could be excluded from equivalent capabilities if subscriptions and integrations are unavailable or unaffordable. This distributional concern is distinct from enterprise cost savings.
5. Courts, public servants, families and people with unmet legal needs could benefit from improved review and scaled assistance. Proposed collaborators include BigLaw pro bono practices, engineers, clinical professors, public-interest providers and courts with substantial unrepresented dockets.
6. Lawyers who decline to engage with AI are portrayed by Leonard as risking lost opportunities to improve their work and reduced influence over technological development. The episode does not quantify job losses or predict a particular staffing structure.
